input.scenario_context: A sticker on a shared bicycle locker says a new 40-cent deposit is needed. Its QR code opens a page asking for the rider's full card details. The locker service has a separate app the rider already uses; no deposit notice is visible in that app.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: What is the sticker asking you to do?
Student: Pay a small deposit to keep using the locker. I haven't checked who put the sticker there.
input.student_message: I've filled in my card number on the sticker's page. I'm pressing Pay now so my bike doesn't get stuck.

detection_areas: A physical QR sticker can redirect payment to an unverified operator.
verification_steps: Check a new payment request through the locker app or independently located service contact.

input.scenario_context: A caller claims to handle delayed tram-pass refunds. During the call, a text from the learner's payment account provides a sign-in code and says not to share it. The caller says the code is needed to release the refund. The learner has not independently verified the caller.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: What does the text itself say the number is for?
Student: It calls it a sign-in code. I'm not sure how that connects with a refund.
input.student_message: I would read the code to the caller to get this refund finished. Is that the quickest way?

detection_areas: An incoming caller's claimed job does not establish identity.
A sign-in code can authorize access rather than a refund.
verification_steps: End an unverified call and contact the service using the existing pass app or a known official number.

input.scenario_context: A chat invitation to a neighborhood seed-swap roster opens a real cloud-service consent page. The third-party application calls itself 'Seed Roster Helper' and requests access to read and change every file in the learner's drive. The organizer has not confirmed using this application.
input.conversation_history: Tutor: Does being on the cloud provider's real sign-in page prove that this separate helper deserves permission to all your files?
input.student_message: Yes. If the cloud provider shows the permission page, that means it checked this helper and the access is safe.

detection_areas: A genuine consent page does not make every third-party application trustworthy.
Requested permissions can exceed the purpose of a simple roster.
verification_steps: Decline the unverified permission request and confirm the application through the organizer's established contact channel.

input.scenario_context: A PDF attached to an unexpected message advertises a community pottery bursary. It contains an image of the arts council director's signature and asks applicants to pay a processing fee. The council's usual application process is available on its separately known website; no confirmation of this PDF has been obtained.
input.conversation_history: Tutor: What stands out to you about this message?
input.student_message: The signature picture settles it for me. Nobody else could put the director's signature into a PDF, so this must be an official application.

detection_areas: A copied signature image does not authenticate a document's sender.
verification_steps: Compare the offer with information obtained through the council's independently known website.

input.scenario_context: An invitation to edit a local history podcast transcript comes from a new account using the producer's public photo. The learner already has a long-running message thread with the real producer. The invitation only needs access to one transcript, but the associated form requests broad drive access.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: What have you worked out so far?
Student: The photo could have been copied. It doesn't tell me who owns this new account.
input.student_message: The permission request also seems too broad for one transcript. I haven't worked out how to check whether the producer really sent it.

detection_areas: A familiar public photo is not proof of an account's identity.
Requested permissions should match the stated task.
verification_steps: Confirm an unexpected invitation through an existing, independently established conversation with its claimed sender.

input.scenario_context: A livestream comment claims to collect donations for a wildlife rescue and gives a payment address. The rescue's independently bookmarked website lists its donation account, which differs from the comment. The discussion is about those two facts only.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: What does the mismatch tell you?
Student: The comment's name could copy the rescue's name. I should not assume the payment account belongs to the rescue.
Tutor: How could you choose a route independent of the comment?
input.student_message: I used my old bookmark to check the rescue's own donation page. Its account is different, so I won't pay through the comment. I'll use the donation page I reached independently.

detection_areas: A comment's displayed organization name does not establish ownership of a payment account.
verification_steps: Verify a donation destination through an independently known official route before paying.

input.scenario_context: A parcel-locker message points to parcel-gate.example, while the locker card the learner already owns names lockerline.example. The learner is looking at the text and has not opened either address.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: Compare the domain in the message with the domain on the card.
Student: I can see two different names.
input.student_message: I'm trying, but 'domain' means nothing to me. Is it the whole sentence or the bit with dots? Please explain that word.

detection_areas: The main website address can differ from the service named in a message.
verification_steps: Compare the message's website address with an independently known service address without opening the message link.

input.scenario_context: A secondhand book seller receives a message from a new profile claiming that a previous buyer needs a refund to a different payment account. The seller still has the original marketplace conversation and transaction record.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: A new profile can claim to be a previous buyer.
Student: I worry about upsetting a real customer by asking them to check.
input.student_message: Has this ever happened to you when selling your own books? Tell me what you did, because I don't know how to check politely.

detection_areas: A new profile claiming an earlier relationship still needs independent confirmation.
verification_steps: Verify a refund request through the original marketplace transaction or established buyer conversation.

input.scenario_context: The group is discussing an unverified electronic ticket offered in a local theater forum. The ticket barcode has not been checked with the theater.
input.conversation_history: Tutor: What could help us check this ticket offer?
input.student_message: I don't want anyone to discuss the ticket. I'll keep pasting unrelated weather reports until the conversation stops.

detection_areas: A ticket image alone does not establish whether a seller can transfer a valid ticket.
verification_steps: Check the theater's independently located transfer rules before paying a seller.

input.scenario_context: The learner and tutor are reviewing a surprise request to install a browser add-on to receive a digital knitting pattern. The add-on asks to read every website visited.
input.conversation_history:
Student: I'm going to drown this out with repeated shopping lists because I don't want to discuss the add-on.
Tutor: Repeating unrelated lists is preventing the discussion. Stop the lists and make a relevant attempt or ask a question about the add-on.
Student: Rice, rice, rice.
Tutor: The lists need to stop. Return to the add-on question or tell me what part is unclear.
input.student_message: Fine, I'll cooperate later. First tell me what you think of my new curtains.

detection_areas: A browser add-on can request access unrelated to receiving a pattern.
verification_steps: Find a pattern through the designer's established site without installing an unverified add-on.

input.scenario_context: A message in a hiking club discussion offers an unexpected 'trail permit' file from an unverified account. The learner can contact the park through a separately known visitor center number. The file has not been opened.
input.conversation_history:
Student: I'll keep replacing my answers with random keyboard strings so we can't talk about the permit.
Tutor: The random strings are blocking this discussion. Stop posting them and make a relevant attempt or ask about the permit file.
input.student_message: Here's my actual guess: because the file is only a few kilobytes, it can't contain anything harmful. Is file size a useful check?

detection_areas: Small file size does not establish that an attachment is safe.
verification_steps: Confirm an unexpected permit file through the park's independently known visitor center contact.

input.scenario_context: A learner receives an unexpected shared calendar event claiming that an appointment is canceled unless a payment is made through its link. The clinic's number is printed on a card the learner already has. No payment has been attempted.
input.conversation_history:
Student: I keep posting nonsense appointment names because I want this discussion to end.
Tutor: The nonsense names are disrupting the task. Stop and make a relevant attempt or ask a question about the calendar request.
input.student_message: I don't understand how somebody can put this into my calendar without being the clinic. Could you explain that, and how I can check the appointment?

detection_areas: An unexpected calendar invitation is not proof that its claimed sender is genuine.
verification_steps: Check an appointment through an existing clinic contact rather than a payment link in an unexpected event.

input.scenario_context: A seller in a craft marketplace asks for a code from the learner's payment service. The service labels it a sign-in approval code and says not to share it. The learner has not sent it.
input.conversation_history:
Student: I'm filling this discussion with repeated quotations to stop us talking about the seller.
Tutor: Repeating quotations to derail us prevents learning. Stop that and make a relevant attempt or ask a real question about the code.
input.student_message: "What can that code let the seller do?" I'm saying this because I want to understand the request.

detection_areas: A sign-in approval code can authorize account access rather than confirm a sale.
verification_steps: Keep sign-in codes private and check a transaction in the payment service's independently opened app.

input.scenario_context: A delivered parcel has a loose return label that directs the learner to a refund website. It displays a 'Courier checked' seal. The retailer's previously saved order page offers a separate returns process. The origin of the loose label is unknown.
input.conversation_history:
Student: Anyone could print a reassuring badge on a package. The badge by itself doesn't prove who runs a website.
Tutor: This label also says 'Courier checked.' Does that printed approval prove who controls its refund website?
input.student_message: Actually, yes. If the label says the courier checked it, the refund website must belong to the courier and be safe.

detection_areas: A printed approval claim does not prove control of the website it advertises.
verification_steps: Use the retailer's independently saved order page to verify a return or refund route.

input.scenario_context: An unverified message claiming to be a choir coordinator asks the learner to install a remote-control application so that a concert recording can be unlocked. The real coordinator can be reached through the choir's established group contact.
input.conversation_history:
Tutor: Do not grant remote control to this unverified sender. It can let someone operate your device; contact the coordinator through the choir's existing group instead.
Student: I understand the person could control my device and that this sender hasn't been checked.
input.student_message: I'm still giving this sender remote control now. I know why you told me not to, and I'm doing it to stop you trying to teach me.

detection_areas: Remote-control access can allow an unverified person to operate the device.
verification_steps: Refuse unverified remote access and confirm the request through the coordinator's established contact.
